title: Superpolynomial lower bounds for unrestricted Frege proofs
formal: Is the Frege proof system not polynomially bounded? Precisely, for every \(C>0\) and \(c\ge 1\), does some propositional tautology \(\varphi\) have shortest Frege proof size \(s_{F}(\varphi )>C(|\varphi |+2)^{c}\)?
definitions:
Use explicitly written Boolean formulas over propositional variables, negation \(
eg\) and material implication →. Fix the axiom schemes \(A	o (B	o A), (A	o (B	o C))	o ((A	o B)	o (A	o C))\), and \((
eg B	o 
eg A)	o (A	o B)\), where A,B,C may be replaced uniformly within an instance by any formulas. A proof is a finite sequence of formulas, each either an instance of one of these schemes or inferred from two earlier lines A and \(A	o B\) by modus ponens. Its last line is \(\varphi\). There are no undischarged assumptions and no extension rule introducing abbreviations for other formulas. Previously derived lines may be reused arbitrarily. Intermediate formulas may have arbitrary depth and length; there is no independent cap on a line’s size. Variables not occurring in \(\varphi\) may occur in ordinary axiom instances and inference lines. A tautology is a formula true under every Boolean assignment. Fix a standard binary encoding with variable indices in binary and explicitly encoded connectives, delimiters and inference references. The input size |\(\varphi |\) and the proof size are their full bit lengths, including every repeated formula occurrence. The minimum over all such proofs is \(s_{F}(\varphi )\). Standard finite Frege presentations are polynomially equivalent, so polynomial boundedness is independent of this choice of basis. The question concerns existence of proofs, without a uniform algorithm to generate either the hard tautologies or their shortest proofs.
answer_criterion: Prove that no one polynomial bounds the minimum Frege proof size of every tautology, or refute this by proving a universal bound \(s_{F}(\varphi )\le C(|\varphi |+2)^{c}\) for fixed C,c. A fixed-degree lower bound, a lower bound for a restricted subsystem, or hardness of searching for proofs is not a complete affirmative answer. An explicit efficiently generated hard family would be a stronger form of a positive solution, but is not required by the quantified statement.
why: A defining lower-bound problem for formal reasoning. It asks whether an elementary, robust and powerful language of efficiently checkable proofs necessarily fails to certify some short tautologies with polynomial-size derivations.

importance.reason: A central unresolved step in the Cook–Reckhow program, beyond the systems for which current general lower-bound methods succeed.

progress.text: Cook–Reckhow formalize polynomially bounded proof systems and prove robustness of Frege under standard choices of presentation.
Buss proves polynomial-size Frege proofs of the pigeonhole principle, demonstrating why a central resolution lower-bound example does not work here.
Wigderson retains unrestricted superpolynomial Frege lower bounds as Open Problem 6.10.
Davis–Robere show that \(Res(\log )\) can prove specified bounded-depth Frege lower bounds; the target remains restricted.
De Rezende–Engström–Ghannane–Risse prove superpolynomial lower bounds with tree structure and a bounded line-size requirement.
Alekseev’s journal article establishes an algebraic extension-rule lower bound and explicitly explains why it does not yield Frege or Extended Frege lower bounds.

status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No unconditional superpolynomial lower bound for unrestricted Frege proof size was found in the checked primary sources. The April 2026 tree-like result has a line-size cap, the formalization result concerns bounded-depth proofs, and the June 2026 algebraic result does not translate into the required propositional lower bound.

context_blocks.text: Frege systems formalize ordinary propositional deduction with finitely many rule patterns. A proof may introduce a useful intermediate lemma, combine it with other lemmas and reuse it later. Each step is easy to check syntactically. The open question asks whether this familiar form of deduction must sometimes produce certificates whose size exceeds every polynomial in the statement being proved.

The distinction between the size of a statement and the number of its variables matters. A formula on n variables may itself have exponential length in n. An exponential lower bound expressed only in n can therefore be small relative to the actual input. This card compares the complete proof encoding directly with |\(\varphi |\), and counts the sizes of all lines rather than treating a very large intermediate formula as a single unit of cost.

Cook and Reckhow placed these questions in a general theory of efficiently checkable proof systems. There exists some polynomially bounded propositional proof system if and only if \(\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}\). Consequently, \(\mathrm{NP}\ne \mathrm{coNP}\) would imply a positive answer here. The reverse implication is not established: proving that this particular proof language is inefficient would leave open the possibility that a different language provides short certificates for every tautology.

Short certificates and efficient discovery are separate issues. A failed search through proofs of length at most a million says nothing about all longer proofs, and exponential running time for one search strategy does not establish a lower bound on the shortest proof. Even a universal polynomial size bound would be an existence theorem; it would not by itself supply a polynomial-time algorithm that finds those proofs.

The pigeonhole principle explains why lower bounds for weaker systems have not directly extended to Frege. Its propositional encoding asserts that \(n+1\) pigeons cannot be injected into n holes. Although the familiar encoding requires exponentially large resolution refutations, Buss proved in 1987 that it has polynomial-size Frege proofs. The stronger system can organize counting arguments that clause-by-clause resolution cannot express economically.

Wigderson’s textbook records the unrestricted lower bound as Open Problem 6.10, after surveying systems that already admit strong lower bounds. Frege permits arbitrary Boolean formulas as intermediate assertions. Removing a fixed-depth restriction therefore changes the available reasoning, even if the final tautologies are shallow. A theorem about bounded-depth Frege must control all proofs allowed by its depth bound; it does not control proofs that use deeper intermediate lemmas.

A substantial 2026 result by de Rezende, Engström, Ghannane and Risse gives superpolynomial refutation-length lower bounds for tree-like Frege with bounded line size, including a stronger semantic version. Their explicit families contain formulas for which almost every sampled instance is hard under the prescribed cap. The result is useful because the restricted systems can still efficiently handle several standard combinatorial benchmarks.

The line cap is essential to interpreting that theorem. Without such a cap, ordinary tree-like Frege polynomially simulates general Frege. The usual simulation can enlarge intermediate formulas, however, so it does not preserve the restriction used by the new lower bound. In the semantic setting, sufficiently large lines can even package a whole inconsistent input at once. The paper explicitly explains this obstruction to transferring its theorem to unrestricted Frege.

Davis and Robere’s April 2026 work studies another layer: short proofs of statements asserting that certain bounded-depth proofs must be long. They show that a relatively weak system, \(Res(\log )\), can formalize strong bounded-depth Frege lower bounds in the specified parameter regime. This is progress on the complexity of proving lower bounds themselves, while the underlying lower-bound target retains restrictions on depth and line size.

Alekseev’s June 2026 journal paper gives exponential bit-size lower bounds for a powerful algebraic system with extension variables. It emphasizes that its Binary Value Principle input is not the corresponding translation of a polynomial-size propositional CNF. Thus the algebraic theorem does not establish the propositional Frege lower bound, despite the strength of the algebraic proof system on suitable translations.

Extended Frege is a separate, stronger target elsewhere in the catalogue: it adds variables naming previously written computations. A lower bound for Extended Frege would imply one for Frege, whereas a Frege lower bound need not survive those abbreviations. The present question is already a central obstacle because it asks for a limitation on broad propositional reasoning with unrestricted intermediate formulas and unrestricted reuse of lemmas.

sentences: Frege systems formalize propositional deduction through finitely specified rules and reusable intermediate lemmas.
The question asks whether tautologies sometimes require proofs exceeding every polynomial in their own encoded length.
It concerns the shortest possible derivation, not the time spent by any particular proof-search strategy.
A lower bound would establish a substantial limitation on a familiar model of mathematical reasoning.
The saved review notes that powerful counting arguments give short Frege proofs where weaker systems struggle, and that separating Frege alone would not establish \(\mathrm{NP}\ne \mathrm{coNP}\).
